title: Ultrasonic Testing for Wind Turbines | UT Inspection (US)
description: Ultrasonic inspection of onshore wind tower welds, flanges, tower bolts, main shafts and gearbox housings across the US wind belt. Request a UT quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Wind Turbines: Tower Weld, Bolt and Shaft UT Inspection in the US
html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic testing (UT) on onshore wind turbine steel in the United States: tower flange and circumferential welds, tower and anchor bolts, main shafts, gearbox and bearing housings, and nacelle frames. We mobilize technicians to a tower fabrication plant, a laydown yard or a turbine site for the agreed scope. Blade inspection is composite work and is not part of what we offer. Request a UT inspection quote with the component list, drawings and site address.

Why wind turbine steel needs ultrasonic examination

A modern onshore turbine stands on a rolled and welded steel tube that may carry the nacelle, rotor and gearbox a hundred meters or more above the ground, and it does so through millions of load cycles. The weld seams and flange connections are the fatigue-critical points. A small planar flaw buried in a circumferential weld can grow for years before it shows on the surface, which is why volumetric examination is specified during tower fabrication and why owners sometimes order it again after a bolt failure, a lightning strike or an unusual load event. Ultrasonic testing is the practical field method: it finds internal planar flaws such as lack of fusion and cracks, and it reads wall thickness, all from one side of the steel.

UT does not replace surface methods. Cracks at the toe of a nacelle frame weld, or in the thread roots of a bolt, are found more reliably by magnetic particle inspection for wind turbines, and nonmagnetic or coated parts call for liquid penetrant testing for wind turbines. We recommend a combination when the part geometry makes one method alone uncertain. Our national ultrasonic testing page explains how the method works in general.

Tower flange and circumferential weld inspection

Wind towers are built from tapered cans, which are rolled plate with a longitudinal seam, joined end to end by circumferential welds, with a heavy forged or rolled flange welded to each end. Fabrication shops examine those welds by ultrasonic testing, usually under AWS D1.1 or the turbine manufacturer's own specification, which sets scan technique, sensitivity and acceptance. We examine the weld metal and heat-affected zone with shear wave transducers at the angles the procedure specifies, scan from both sides where geometry allows, and record the position and length of any indication against the drawing. Door frames and internal platform attachments, which concentrate stress, are added to the scope on request.

Flange welds deserve special attention. The flange-to-can weld is a transition from a thick forging to thinner shell plate, and the geometry is awkward for scanning. We take the weld profile, check that the scan plan covers the root, and verify flange flatness and plate lamination with straight beam readings where the specification calls for them. Our detailed page on ultrasonic weld inspection sets out the technique and the reporting format that applies to wind tower welds.

Tower bolts, anchor bolts and flange connections

Tower sections are bolted together through flange rings, and the whole structure sits on a foundation anchor cage. When a bolt fails, the first question is whether others are cracked. Ultrasonic bolt examination uses a transducer on the bolt head or stud end; a sound pulse travels the length of the fastener and returns from the far end, and a crack in the shank or thread run-out shows as an echo from a position other than the end. The same reading, compared with a reference, gives bolt length change and can indicate stretch. It can screen a large number of bolts quickly with the nacelle or tower section still assembled, and the results go to the owner's engineer to decide on retorque, replacement or further examination.

We need to know bolt diameter, length, grade and head type, plus the access: bolt heads inside a tower base may be easy to reach, while those at an upper section flange can require climbing under the owner's fall protection plan. Anchor bolts below grade are tested only where the top is exposed. We do not evaluate preload, which is a torque or tension question for the turbine manufacturer, and our technicians do not retorque bolts.

Main shafts, gearbox and bearing housings

The main shaft is a forging that carries rotor loads into the drive train. Ultrasonic inspection is used on shafts during fabrication to find forging defects and, on in-service shafts, when an owner wants to rule out fatigue cracking near a bearing seat or a fillet. Examination requires a clean, accessible surface, so the shaft often has to be exposed during a major component replacement. Gearbox housings and bearing housings are castings or fabricated steel parts, and ultrasonic work on them looks for casting discontinuities and wall thickness at sealing surfaces. The geometry is tricky, so we work from the manufacturer's drawing and a scan plan agreed in advance. Our page on ultrasonic testing of castings and forgings covers that technique in more detail, though the rules for a given shaft come from the owner or manufacturer.

Nacelle frames and bedplates

The nacelle frame, or bedplate, is a heavy welded or cast structure that holds the drive train. Welds at stiffeners and mounting pads are examined by UT for internal flaws and by MT or PT at the surface. These are often examined in a shop or laydown yard after fabrication or repair. We scan the welds listed on the manufacturer's weld map to the specified acceptance level and keep the map as part of the report.

Technique: calibration, couplant and weather

Wind sites are cold, damp and windy, and technique must allow for that. We calibrate on blocks suited to the steel and the angle, verify sensitivity with a reference reflector before each part, and recheck at intervals during long scans and at the end. Couplant is chosen for the temperature: a low-temperature gel works in cold weather, and a cleaner, scraped surface prevents spurious signals. Painted tower surfaces are scanned through the coating only if the procedure accounts for the loss; otherwise paint is removed at the scan path. Rust and weld spatter are removed to bare metal where shear wave contact is needed.

Inside a tower, the air is still but cramped, with limited lighting; outside, wind speed can stop work at height. We follow the site's climbing and rescue rules and OSHA fall protection requirements, and we ask the owner to confirm the access method, whether crane, lift, platform or rope access, as it is arranged by the site and not by us.

Codes, specifications and acceptance

Wind tower fabrication relies on AWS D1.1 for structural steel welding, ASTM material specifications for plate and forgings, and the turbine manufacturer's requirements, which often exceed the code. Acceptance criteria come from those documents, not from Atlantis. Our report names the specification and revision used. The AWS guide for ultrasonic examination of welds in structural steel and the ASME Section V approach are both useful references; see our explainer of ASME Section V Article 4 for how a UT procedure is structured, and the ultimate guide to ultrasonic testing for the physics.

Who performs the work and how it is approved

Examiners are mobilized under a written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The examiner on the tower is a Level II who sets up, scans and evaluates; the procedure and the finished report pass to an ASNT Level III for approval. We prepare a scan plan for each tower type before work starts, so the same technique is repeated on every can and flange in a production run. If a fabricator or owner has its own qualified procedure, we work to it and ask only that it be provided with the quote request. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001, and the report format follows the same record-keeping every time, with the drawing reference and revision on the first page.

What the report contains

  • Project, turbine or tower serial number and component identifiers
  • Procedure number and revision, and the specification used for acceptance
  • Instrument, transducer angle and frequency, couplant and calibration blocks
  • Weld map or bolt list with positions scanned
  • Technician name and qualification level
  • Each indication with location, length, depth and amplitude, and accept or reject
  • Coverage limits, surface condition and ambient temperature

What to send for a quote

  • Weld maps, drawings and the manufacturer's specification
  • Component list: tower sections, bolts, shafts, housings, with quantities
  • Material grades and thicknesses
  • Whether the work is in a plant or at the turbine site
  • Access method, fall protection plan and rescue arrangements
  • Schedule window, site orientation or badging requirements and the address

What we do not do

Atlantis does not inspect turbine blades, which are composite structures requiring different methods. We do not perform radiography in the United States because it is licensed under 10 CFR Part 34 or Agreement State rules. We do not offer specialist techniques on this page, and we do not calculate fatigue life or decide on repair; the owner, manufacturer or engineer does that with our data.

Where we work in the US for wind energy

  • Omaha: Nebraska and Iowa wind projects within reach of Plains fabrication shops.
  • Wichita: Kansas wind farms and heavy steel fabricators.
  • Oklahoma City: Oklahoma wind belt projects.
  • Denver: Colorado and Wyoming wind and the Front Range steel fabricators.
  • Midland: West Texas wind farms in the Permian region.
  • Tulsa: Northeast Oklahoma fabrication and nearby wind projects.
  • Minneapolis: Minnesota and the Dakotas, where cold weather shapes the work.
  • Albuquerque: New Mexico wind and high-altitude conditions.

Training your own technicians

Fabricators and owner-operators who want routine UT in house can begin with UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, then use the ultrasonic simulator to practice weld scans. The manufacturing NDT training page covers fabrication-shop needs. Since the employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A, a written practice and a procedure from NDT technical procedure development are the foundation.

faq.q: Can UT find cracks in wind turbine tower bolts?
faq.a: Yes. A transducer on the head or end of the bolt sends a pulse down its length, and a crack in the shank or thread run-out returns an echo before the far end. It screens many bolts quickly, but the owner's engineer decides on retorque or replacement.

faq.q: Which tower welds are examined by ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Circumferential welds between tower cans, flange-to-can welds, longitudinal seams and door frame or platform attachments. The specification, often AWS D1.1 or the turbine manufacturer's document, sets which welds, how far to scan and what is acceptable.

No. Blades are fiberglass and carbon composite, and their inspection uses different methods that Atlantis does not offer. We inspect the steel and iron parts: towers, bolts, shafts, housings and frames.

faq.q: How do you get to the part on a tower?
faq.a: The site arranges access by crane, lift, platform or rope, under its own fall protection and rescue plan. Our technicians follow it and OSHA requirements. We do not supply cranes, rope teams or scaffolding.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects an indication in a tower weld?
faq.a: Acceptance comes from the governing specification named in the report, such as AWS D1.1 or the manufacturer's requirement. Atlantis reports against those criteria; the owner, manufacturer or engineer makes decisions about repair.

faq.q: Can you test a weld through paint?
faq.a: Sometimes, if the procedure accounts for signal loss through the coating and the paint is well bonded. If it is flaking or thick, we remove it along the scan path so contact is reliable.

faq.q: What do you need to quote tower weld inspection?
faq.a: Weld maps and drawings, the specification, material and thickness, number of welds or towers, location and access method, schedule window and site requirements such as badging.

faq.q: Is cold weather a problem for ultrasonic work?
faq.a: It changes technique, not feasibility. We use couplant rated for low temperatures, keep instruments within their operating range and calibrate more often. Extreme wind or ice at height can stop work until the site says it is safe.

faq.q: Do you test main shafts while they are in the nacelle?
faq.a: Only where access allows a clean, scannable surface. Usually the shaft is exposed during a major component change. We work from the manufacturer's drawing and plan, and findings go to the owner or manufacturer for decision.
